extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, legal researchers, and historians of journalism; also journalists and newswire managers studying historical wire-service practices
extracted.subtask_description: Affidavits and sworn testimony describing early 20th-century news‑wireroom practices (tipping, code words, rewriting, eavesdropping risk) in the Associated Press vs. International News Service litigation. Records operational customs about how stories were obtained, reported, credited, and distributed across bureaus and trunk lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'tip'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tip', in news service parlance, means a despatch containing, in a brief manner, the substance of the nature and character of a story and is frequently accompanied by an indication as to its point of origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tips may be brief flashes outlining an event or more extended reports; when sufficiently complete they enable a central office to write and send a story from the tip itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tips sufficient to permit central office to re-write without independent inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Very frequently these tips sent out were sufficiently complete as to the nature and character of the story and its point of origin to enable the central office ... to re-write the information, and then send it out over its own wires ... without making any independent investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include tips that allowed the Associated Press to send bulletins based directly on material received from another service; such tips often resulted in prompt bulletins to subscribers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to notify central office when 'opposition' is carrying a story
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a custom (and, in some offices, an order) that any time a news story of any importance broke and came to the attention of the operators and employees, and when it appeared the news department was not getting the story on the wires quickly, they should promptly tip off the news department at the nearest bureau office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice was intended so 'the story could be promptly handled' and to prevent one service being beaten by another; such tips were routed to headquarters and often produced immediate bulletins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit/advancement for sending tips
rubrics_metrics.description: The bulletin ... stated that any tips so sent out would be credited to the operator sending the same, and would count in his advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operators were motivated to send tips; the office practice rewarded proactive tipsters by crediting and counting tips in promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of code words to identify source services
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees used code words to designate the opposition services which were carrying matter which the United Press/Associated Press did not have; e.g., the code word 'Appleton's' for an Associated Press despatch, 'Henderson's' for Hearst/National News Association, or prefacing messages with 'Opposition says'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code prefacing indicated to central offices which organization was carrying the story, enabling appropriate handling without naming the rival outright in routine trunk messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine practice of rewriting published items from other papers and sending as service dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: It was the universal custom among newspaper men, and among news services, to utilize the facts which are set forth in any published story, to rewrite that story, if they see fit, and to send it out to whom, and as they see fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Atlanta Georgian items were rewritten and sent as Associated Press dispatches; Washington bureau staff read local papers and re-sent items of sufficient importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignoring original source when rewriting opposition material
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of any items rewritten from opposition papers was absolutely ignored ... if an article should appear ... accompanied by a notice that it had been received through the International News Service, no reference to that fact would be made in the story, as subsequently rewritten and sent out by the Associated Press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewritten matter was distributed without crediting the originating news service or newspaper; this was described as a common and invariable practice unless authenticity was in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting exclusive stories with minimal changes (lead revisions) and transmitting as own
rubrics_metrics.description: I frequently took these exclusive stories ... revised or re-wrote fifty or a hundred words of the first part of the story, commonly called the 'lead' and pasted up the rest of the story to the revised 'lead', and then transmitted the same on the wire ... The stories which I obtained and transmitted ... were substantially the stories which I took from the Sun, excepting for a change in the 'lead'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Fred Harvey: exclusive cables from the Laffan Bureau (New York Sun) were lightly revised and sent over AP special wires; copy was routinely sent to the local superintendent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining multiple published accounts into a single dispatch
rubrics_metrics.description: On one occasion ... I received for transmission a story which had been rewritten from articles published both in the Herald and the Examiner ... This story combined in one article the important features of the Herald story and the important features of the Examiner story, and went out ... as an Associated Press news despatch, without any indication as to its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors sometimes merged details from multiple competitors' accounts and issued a unified dispatch as their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational routing and trunk-wire messaging about 'opposition' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages were constantly going and coming over the trunk wires ... notifying the central office that 'Opposition' was carrying such and such a story and thereafter bulletins ... would come back from the Central Office ... containing the story, or a bulletin thereof, as to which the Central Office had been tipped off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trunk-wire alerts informed headquarters that rival services had a story so central office could respond rapidly; such notices often used code words rather than naming the rival service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to eavesdropping via loud sounder operation
rubrics_metrics.description: The loud sounder is a part of the ordinary telegraph outfit, and its clicks can be heard by any one of ordinary hearing ... Mr. Wilson's instrument was approximately and not more than ten feet from my instrument. A telegraph instrument in operation with a loud sounder can easily be heard by a person of average hearing at a greater distance than ten feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony indicates that use of the loud sounder in shared anterooms permitted adjacent operators to hear despatches as they came over another service's wire, enabling informal 'taking' of material as it arrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central office practice to promptly send out stories upon receipt of tips
rubrics_metrics.description: On receipt of such tips, the central office of the organization to whom they were addressed did, very frequently, send out the story to which it had been tipped off, very promptly, in order to get to its subscribers the story for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt re-broadcasting was standard to secure speed advantage even when the story originated elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local bureau managers' duty to notify headquarters about opposition coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: It has always been the practice, and it is part of the duties of a local or district bureau manager, to promptly advise his headquarters whenever an opposition service is carrying a story which is of unusual interest and which the bureau office has not yet received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural duty was aimed at preventing being 'beaten' by other services; it applied across divisions and was enforced via trunk messages and code words.
